cards.front: An angle is measured in [ ___ ]; the point where its arms meet is the [ ___ ].
cards.back: An angle is measured in degrees; the point where its arms meet is the vertex.

options.text: An angle is measured in degrees; the point where its arms meet is the vertex.
options.explanation: Degrees quantify the amount of turning between the two arms of an angle. The vertex is their shared endpoint, where the two arms meet.

options.text: An angle is measured in degrees; the point where its arms meet is the centre.
options.explanation: Calling this point the centre confuses angle terminology with circles. Angles are measured in degrees, and the shared endpoint of their arms is called the vertex.

options.text: An angle is measured in centimetres; the point where its arms meet is the vertex.
options.explanation: Centimetres measure length rather than turning. An angle is measured in degrees, while the point at which its two arms meet is correctly called the vertex.

options.text: An angle is measured in centimetres; the point where its arms meet is the endpoint.
options.explanation: This mixes length measurement with imprecise line terminology. Angles are measured in degrees, and the particular shared endpoint where both arms meet is the vertex.

cards.front: A right angle is [ ___ ]; a straight line angle is [ ___ ].
cards.back: A right angle is 90°; a straight line angle is 180°.

options.text: A right angle is 90°; a straight line angle is 180°.
options.explanation: A quarter turn measures 90°, so it forms a right angle. A half turn measures 180°, producing an angle along a straight line.

options.text: A right angle is 180°; a straight line angle is 90°.
options.explanation: These values have been reversed. A right angle is a quarter turn, or 90°, whereas an angle on a straight line is a half turn, or 180°.

options.text: A right angle is 45°; a straight line angle is 180°.
options.explanation: The straight line value is correct, but 45° is half a right angle. A complete right angle is a quarter turn and therefore measures 90°.

options.text: A right angle is 90°; a straight line angle is 360°.
options.explanation: The right-angle value is correct, but 360° represents a full turn. A straight line makes only a half turn, so its angle is 180°.

cards.front: Classify an angle of 40°.

options.text: Acute.
options.explanation: An acute angle is greater than 0° but less than 90°. Since 40° lies within that interval, it is classified as acute.

options.text: Right.
options.explanation: A right angle must measure exactly 90°, not merely less than 90°. Since 40° is between 0° and 90°, the correct classification is acute.

options.text: Obtuse.
options.explanation: An obtuse angle is greater than 90° but less than 180°. Since 40° is below 90°, it is an acute angle instead.

options.text: Reflex.
options.explanation: A reflex angle is greater than 180° but less than 360°. Since 40° is much smaller than 180°, it is classified as acute.

cards.front: Classify an angle of 130°.

options.text: Obtuse.
options.explanation: An obtuse angle is greater than 90° but less than 180°. Since 130° lies within this interval, its correct classification is obtuse.

options.text: Acute.
options.explanation: Acute angles are smaller than 90°. Since 130° is greater than 90° but less than 180°, the correct classification is obtuse.

options.text: Reflex.
options.explanation: Reflex angles are greater than 180°. Since 130° lies between 90° and 180°, it is obtuse rather than reflex.

options.text: Right.
options.explanation: A right angle measures exactly 90°. Since 130° exceeds 90° without reaching 180°, it must be classified as an obtuse angle.

cards.front: Classify an angle of 245°.

options.text: Reflex.
options.explanation: A reflex angle is greater than 180° but less than 360°. Since 245° lies in that range, it is correctly classified as reflex.

options.text: Obtuse.
options.explanation: Obtuse angles are between 90° and 180°. Since 245° is greater than 180° but less than 360°, it is a reflex angle.

options.text: Acute.
options.explanation: Acute angles are smaller than 90°, so this classification ignores the angle’s much larger turn. At 245°, the angle is correctly classified as reflex.

options.text: Straight.
options.explanation: A straight angle measures exactly 180°. Since 245° extends 65° beyond a straight angle, it falls in the reflex-angle range.

cards.front: What tool is used to measure or draw angles?

options.text: A protractor.
options.explanation: A protractor has a degree scale designed for measuring existing angles and marking given angles accurately when drawing them.

options.text: A compass.
options.explanation: A compass draws circles and arcs but does not provide a degree scale for measuring angles. The appropriate measuring and drawing tool is a protractor.

options.text: A ruler.
options.explanation: A ruler measures lengths and draws straight lines, but it has no degree scale. Angles are measured or marked out using a protractor.

options.text: A set square.
options.explanation: A set square provides only certain fixed angles, commonly 30°, 45°, 60° and 90°. A protractor measures or draws angles of varied sizes.

cards.front: When measuring an angle, where should the protractor's centre go?

options.text: On the vertex.
options.explanation: The protractor’s centre must coincide with the angle’s vertex so that its baseline and degree scale measure the turn accurately from the correct point.

options.text: On the 0° mark.
options.explanation: The 0° mark is used to choose the correct scale, not to position the centre. The protractor’s centre should be placed directly on the angle’s vertex.

options.text: On the middle of one arm.
options.explanation: Placing the centre partway along an arm shifts the measuring point and produces an incorrect reading. The centre must be aligned with the vertex.

options.text: On the end of one arm.
options.explanation: The end of an arm is not the point from which the angle opens. The protractor’s centre must be placed on the vertex where both arms meet.

cards.front: On a protractor, read from the [ ___ ] that lies on [ ___ ].
cards.back: On a protractor, read from the 0° line that lies on one arm of the angle.

options.text: On a protractor, read from the 0° line that lies on one arm of the angle.
options.explanation: The correct scale begins at 0° on the arm aligned with the protractor’s baseline. Following that scale to the other arm gives the angle’s measurement.

options.text: On a protractor, read from the 180° line that lies on one arm of the angle.
options.explanation: Starting at 180° selects the scale in the wrong direction and commonly gives the supplementary reading. Begin with the 0° line aligned to one arm.

options.text: On a protractor, read from the 0° line that lies on the curved edge of the protractor.
options.explanation: The curved edge contains the numbered scales but is not aligned with the angle. The relevant 0° line must lie along one arm of the angle.

options.text: On a protractor, read from the 90° line that lies on the other arm of the angle.
options.explanation: The 90° line is a fixed quarter-turn reference, not the starting line for general measurements. Start from the 0° line aligned with one arm.

cards.front: After marking 110° with a protractor, how do you complete the angle?
cards.back: Draw a straight line from the vertex through the mark.

options.text: Draw a straight line from the vertex through the mark.
options.explanation: The second arm must begin at the same vertex as the first arm and pass through the 110° mark to form the measured angle.

options.text: Draw a straight line from the mark to the end of the first arm.
options.explanation: Joining the mark to the first arm’s endpoint creates a line that does not start at the vertex. The second arm must run from the vertex through the mark.

options.text: Draw a curved line from the vertex through the mark.
options.explanation: An angle is formed by two straight arms sharing a vertex, not by a curved arm. Draw a straight line from the vertex through the mark.

options.text: Draw a straight line from the mark to the protractor’s centre.
options.explanation: The protractor’s centre should already be positioned over the vertex, so drawing towards it does not create the second arm. Draw from the vertex through the 110° mark.

cards.front: Angles on a straight line add to [ ___ ].
cards.back: Angles on a straight line add to 180°.

options.explanation: A straight line represents half of a complete 360° turn, so all adjacent angles lying along it have a total of 180°.
A full turn totals 360°, which applies to angles around a point. Angles forming a straight line make half a turn, so they add to 180°.
The value 90° is a quarter turn and describes a right angle. A straight line is a half turn, so its angles total 180°.
The value 270° represents three-quarters of a turn rather than a straight line. A straight line is half a turn and therefore measures 180°.

cards.front: A straight line is split into 127° and $x$. Find $x$.

options.explanation: Angles on a straight line add to 180°. Therefore, subtracting the known angle gives $x=180°-127°=53°$.
This results from subtracting 127° from 170° rather than 180°. Angles on a straight line total 180°, so $x=180°-127°=53°$.
This is caused by an arithmetic slip in the subtraction. Using the straight-line total correctly gives $x=180°-127°=53°$, not 63°.
Adding 127° and 180° confuses the required operation. The two adjacent angles must total 180°, so the missing angle is $180°-127°=53°$.

cards.front: Perpendicular lines meet at a [ ___ ], which is [ ___ ].
cards.back: Perpendicular lines meet at a right angle, which is 90°.

options.text: Perpendicular lines meet at a right angle, which is 90°.
options.explanation: Perpendicular lines intersect to form four equal right angles. Each right angle is one-quarter of a full 360° turn, so it measures 90°.

options.text: Perpendicular lines meet at an obtuse angle, which is 90°.
options.explanation: Although 90° is the correct measurement, an angle of exactly 90° is a right angle, not an obtuse angle. Perpendicular lines meet at right angles.

options.text: Perpendicular lines meet at a right angle, which is 180°.
options.explanation: The angle type is correct, but 180° is a straight angle rather than a right angle. Perpendicular lines intersect at 90°.

options.text: Perpendicular lines meet at an acute angle, which is 180°.
options.explanation: An acute angle is less than 90°, while 180° is a straight angle. Perpendicular lines instead meet at a right angle measuring 90°.

cards.front: A right angle is split into 34° and $x$. Find $x$.

options.explanation: A right angle measures 90°, so its two parts must total 90°. Therefore, $x=90°-34°=56°$.
This comes from subtracting 34° incorrectly from 100° rather than using the right-angle total. The correct calculation is $90°-34°=56°$.
Adding 34° to 90° gives an angle larger than the whole right angle. The missing part must be found by $90°-34°=56°$.
This reflects a subtraction error, often treating 90 as if its units digit were larger than 4. Correct borrowing gives $90°-34°=56°$.

cards.front: Angles around a point add to what?

options.explanation: Angles around a point form one complete turn. Since a complete turn measures 360°, all the angles around the point add to 360°.
The value 180° is only half a turn and is the total for angles on a straight line. Around a point, the angles complete a full 360° turn.
The value 90° is one-quarter of a complete turn and represents a right angle. Angles around a point make a full turn totalling 360°.
The value 540° combines one and a half turns, so it exceeds the total around a single point. One complete turn contains exactly 360°.

cards.front: Angles around a point are 90°, 105°, 118° and $x$. Find $x$.

options.explanation: Angles around a point total 360°. The known angles sum to $90°+105°+118°=313°$, leaving $x=360°-313°=47°$.
This follows from misadding the known angles as 303° instead of 313°. Their correct total is 313°, so $x=360°-313°=47°$.
This omits the 90° angle and subtracts only 105° and 118° from 360°. All three known angles must be included, giving $x=47°$.
This is the total of the three known angles, not the missing angle. Subtract that subtotal from 360° to obtain $x=47°$.

cards.front: The three angles inside any triangle add to [ ___ ].
cards.back: The three angles inside any triangle add to 180°.

options.explanation: The interior angles of every triangle have a fixed total of 180°, regardless of the triangle’s side lengths or individual angle sizes.
The value 360° is the total around a point, not inside a triangle. The three interior angles of every triangle add to 180°.
The value 90° is the measure of one right angle and can be a single triangle angle. It is not the total, which is always 180°.
The value 270° is three-quarters of a complete turn and is too large for a triangle’s interior-angle total. The correct total is 180°.

cards.front: A triangle has angles 66°, 41° and $x$. Find $x$.

options.explanation: Angles in a triangle total 180°. Subtracting 66° and 41° gives $x = 180° - 66° - 41° = 73°$.
Adding 66° and 41° gives 107°, but that is the sum of the known angles, not the missing angle. Subtracting 107° from 180° gives 73°.
This results from an arithmetic slip when subtracting the known angles. Since triangle angles total 180°, the calculation is $180° - 66° - 41° = 73°$.
This subtracts only the 41° angle from 180° and ignores the 66° angle. Both known angles must be subtracted, giving $x = 73°$.

cards.front: In an isosceles triangle, equal sides imply what about the base angles?

options.text: The base angles are equal.
options.explanation: In an isosceles triangle, the two equal sides are opposite two equal angles. These opposite angles are the base angles, so they have the same size.

options.text: The base angles are supplementary.
options.explanation: Supplementary angles total 180°, but the base angles of an isosceles triangle do not generally do this. Equal sides imply that the opposite base angles are equal.

options.text: The base angles are perpendicular.
options.explanation: Perpendicular lines meet at 90°, which is unrelated to the equal-side property of an isosceles triangle. The angles opposite the equal sides are equal.

options.text: The base angles are unequal.
options.explanation: This reverses the defining angle property of an isosceles triangle. Because the two sides are equal, the angles opposite those sides - the base angles - are equal.

cards.front: An isosceles triangle has base angles 68° and 68°. Find the top angle.

options.explanation: The angles in a triangle sum to 180°. The two base angles total 136°, so the top angle is $180° - 136° = 44°$.
This is the sum of the two base angles, not the remaining angle. Subtracting their total, 136°, from 180° gives the top angle of 44°.
This subtracts only one 68° base angle from 180°. Both base angles must be included, so the top angle is $180° - 68° - 68° = 44°$.
This assumes all three angles are equal because the triangle is isosceles. Only the base angles are equal here, and the angle sum gives a top angle of 44°.

cards.front: A square corner and an equilateral-triangle corner meet at a shared point. Find the combined angle.

options.explanation: A square corner is 90° and an equilateral-triangle corner is 60°. Their combined angle is therefore $90° + 60° = 150°$.
This incorrectly treats the equilateral-triangle corner as 30°. Every interior angle of an equilateral triangle is 60°, so the combined angle is $90° + 60° = 150°$.
This assumes the two corners form a straight angle. Their actual sizes are 90° and 60°, so adding them gives a combined angle of 150°, not 180°.
This uses the reflex angle around the shared point rather than the combined interior angle. The required angle is $90° + 60° = 150°$; the remaining reflex portion is 210°.
